example: Predict K+ movement in a model cell: K+ starts more concentrated inside, and only K+ channels are open. K+ initially leaves by diffusion. The negative charge left inside then attracts K+ inward until the electrical and concentration forces balance.

en.title: Two Gradients Drive Ion Movement
en.learning_objective: Explain how concentration and electrical gradients combine to determine the net movement of an ion across a membrane.
en.simple_explanation: An ion near a neuronal membrane can face two forces. A concentration gradient drives it from higher concentration toward lower concentration. An electrical gradient attracts it toward opposite charge and repels it from like charge. Ion movement also requires a channel that the ion can cross.
en.how_it_works: Suppose K+ is concentrated inside a model cell and K+ channels open. K+ first diffuses outward. Impermeable negative ions remain inside, so the inner membrane surface becomes negative. That electrical difference pulls K+ inward. At the K+ equilibrium potential, the outward concentration force and inward electrical force are equal and opposite, so net K+ movement stops.
en.visual:
K+ high inside
      ↓ concentration force
K+ moves out
      ↑ electrical force
Equal forces → no net movement
en.use_case: When interpreting a membrane-potential diagram, first identify the ion's concentration difference and charge. Then predict the concentration force, the electrical force, and whether a suitable channel is available.
en.expected_result: In the K+ model, opening K+ channels produces an initial outward K+ flow and a negative voltage inside. Net flow stops when the two forces balance.
en.what_to_notice: Equilibrium does not mean that the concentration difference disappears. A very small redistribution of ions can create enough voltage to oppose further net movement, while the bulk solutions remain nearly electrically neutral.
en.common_mistake: Do not predict ion movement from concentration alone. Membrane voltage, ion charge, and channel availability can reinforce, oppose, or prevent that movement.
en.practical_tip: Draw two separate arrows—one for the concentration force and one for the electrical force—before deciding the net direction.
en.question: K+ is more concentrated inside a cell and only K+ channels are open. Why does net outward K+ movement eventually stop?
en.answer: K+ leaving makes the inside negative, creating an inward electrical force that eventually balances the outward concentration force.
